title: Has U.S. Monetary Policy Really Improved? A 150-Year Perspective - Liberty Street Economics
gist: Barnichon and Mesters benchmark 150 years of US monetary policy against the best feasible response to the shocks faced, finding meaningful improvement only in the last thirty years since Volcker. Gains came mainly from better responses to financial crises (early Fed raised rates into panics) and supply shocks (the postwar Fed under-reacted).

insights.claim: Comparing monetary policy across eras requires separating policy quality from the shocks faced, because central bankers do not control their environment and may suffer worse outcomes simply from larger or harder-to-stabilize shocks.
insights.speaker: Regis Barnichon
insights.so_what: Raw inflation/unemployment records, such as the Great Moderation, are weak evidence of policy skill.
insights.locator: Why Is Measuring Monetary Policy Performance So Difficult?

insights.claim: The authors benchmark actual policy against the best feasible response to the shocks faced, implemented through empirically estimated impulse responses to policy and non-policy shocks rather than a fully specified structural model, for a broad class of macro models.
insights.speaker: Regis Barnichon
insights.so_what: The method is model-light, so it can be applied across very different monetary regimes.

insights.claim: Two complementary metrics are produced: the percentage correction to the policy-path response to each shock, and the distance to minimum loss (DML), the avoidable expected squared inflation and unemployment deviations under the best feasible response.
insights.speaker: Regis Barnichon
insights.so_what: One metric grades the reaction function; the other grades the economic cost of its errors.
insights.quote: The policy-path correction thus assesses the reaction function directly, while the distance to minimum loss captures the economic consequences of policy mistakes.

insights.claim: The study covers four periods: Gold Standard (1879-1912), early Fed (1913-41), postwar (1954-84; table labels 1951-84) and post-Volcker (1990-2019), using shocks including bank panics, government spending, energy, inflation expectations, TFP and monetary policy.
insights.speaker: Regis Barnichon
insights.so_what: Note that the sample ends in 2019, so post-2020 inflation and policy are not evaluated.
insights.locator: We apply these measures to four periods

insights.claim: Monetary policy has not steadily improved over 150 years; most gains emerged only after Volcker's disinflation, with little evidence the Fed's systematic response to shocks improved materially before.
insights.speaker: Regis Barnichon
insights.so_what: Challenges the narrative of gradual learning and suggests modern success is institutional and recent, not guaranteed.
insights.quote: There is surprisingly little evidence that the Federal Reserve’s systematic response to macroeconomic shocks improved materially before.

insights.claim: Policy-path corrections stayed above 100 percent on average in the Gold Standard, early Fed and postwar periods, indicating a reaction function far from optimum.
insights.speaker: Regis Barnichon
insights.so_what: Historic policy was not just unlucky but systematically far from the best feasible response.

insights.claim: In the post-Volcker period corrections shrink to an average absolute value of around 30 percent and become statistically insignificant.
insights.speaker: Regis Barnichon
insights.so_what: Modern policy is statistically indistinguishable from the best feasible response on average, though not perfect.
insights.quote: Only in the post-Volcker period do these corrections become substantially smaller—and statistically insignificant—with an average absolute correction of around 30 percent.

insights.claim: Median distance to minimum loss fell from 97.4 in the early Fed (credible set 57-230) to 8.4 in the Gold Standard era, 6.6 post-WWII and 3.2 post-Volcker (1.4-7.2).
insights.speaker: Regis Barnichon
insights.so_what: The early Fed was an extreme outlier in avoidable macro loss, about 30 times the modern level.

insights.claim: The costs of policy mistakes vary dramatically across periods: the early Fed's avoidable losses were far larger than those of the Gold Standard and postwar eras even where reaction-function errors were comparable.
insights.speaker: Regis Barnichon
insights.so_what: The size of the error matters less than the fragility of the economy it hits, such as financial panics.
insights.quote: the policy mistakes in the Early Fed period were far more costly when compared to those in the Gold Standard era and the Post WWII period

insights.claim: The largest improvements in monetary policy came in the response to financial shocks, measured by bank panics.
insights.speaker: Regis Barnichon
insights.so_what: Crisis response is where modern central banking adds most value.
insights.quote: The largest improvements in monetary policy occurred in the response to financial shocks.

insights.claim: In the early Fed, bank panics were followed by higher policy rates; because panics also lowered inflation, real rates rose, making policy contractionary exactly when support was needed.
insights.speaker: Regis Barnichon
insights.so_what: This is the mechanism behind the 1920s-30s policy failure and the large early-Fed DML.
insights.quote: Because banking panics also lowered inflation, the real policy rate increased substantially

insights.claim: The optimal adjustment for early Fed bank panics would have been to lower rates, substantially stabilizing both inflation and unemployment; bank-panic DML in that era was 29.4 of the 97.4 total.
insights.speaker: Regis Barnichon
insights.so_what: Easing into panics is the empirically supported benchmark.

insights.claim: After Volcker the Fed already lowers rates after financial shocks, the estimated adjustment is small and insignificant, and bank-panic DML is just 0.2.
insights.speaker: Regis Barnichon
insights.so_what: Markets can reasonably expect easing in financial stress, consistent with the modern Fed's reaction function.

insights.claim: The postwar Fed's reaction function was almost as far from optimum as the early Fed's, but the failure was reacting too weakly to supply-side disturbances (energy, productivity and inflation-expectation shocks) rather than to financial crises.
insights.speaker: Regis Barnichon
insights.so_what: Policy failures take different forms by era; weak response to supply shocks drives inflation episodes.
insights.quote: Rather than responding poorly to financial crises, the postwar Federal Reserve reacted too weakly to a range of supply-side disturbances

insights.claim: After inflation-expectation shocks, inflation rose steadily but the policy rate responded only weakly, so real rates fell and reinforced inflation; the optimal correction restores a much stronger rate response, consistent with the Taylor principle.
insights.speaker: Regis Barnichon
insights.so_what: Un-anchored expectations plus insufficient rate response is the recipe for persistent inflation.

insights.claim: Postwar corrections for the inflation-expectations shock were 6.9 percent (credible set 2.1-24.9), and the early-Fed inflation-expectations DML was 30.2.
insights.speaker: Regis Barnichon
insights.so_what: Expectation shocks were the most notable single source of postwar policy-path error, though the table layout is hard to parse.
insights.locator: Percentage correction to policy path response

insights.claim: Post-Volcker supply-shock corrections are small and insignificant (energy -0.6, inflation expectations -1.1, DML around 0.1-0.2 each), implying the modern Fed responds near-optimally to supply shocks.
insights.speaker: Regis Barnichon
insights.so_what: Supports the view that energy and supply shocks are manageable under the current reaction function.
insights.locator: Percentage correction to policy path response

insights.claim: Most of the modern improvement reflects better responses to financial and supply shocks, among other developments, rather than just a more favorable environment.
insights.speaker: Regis Barnichon
insights.so_what: Counters the claim that the Great Moderation was mostly luck, at least for the post-Volcker era.
insights.quote: Most of the gains reflect, among other developments, substantially better responses to financial shocks and supply shocks.

insights.claim: Because the evidence ends in 2019 and the improvements are only about thirty years old, the track record of near-optimal policy rests on a short sample, which warrants caution about extrapolating it to future regimes.
insights.speaker: Regis Barnichon
insights.so_what: The modern regime has been tested by few crises of the size seen in the early Fed.
